<reason>A opened with the strongest moral frame — the debt exists, the money exists, only courts can collect given the veto — and closed with a clever catch that B's own mechanism uses the assets without any judgment. But B won the decisive technical clashes. B caught A migrating from countermeasures (which require reversibility) to permanent transfer without any surviving legal doctrine, caught the "authorizing legislation" concession that blurred A's "courts versus nothing" dichotomy, and sustained a cross-jurisdictional queue/allocation critique A never fully answered. Most decisively, when A's safeguard for "who decides aggression" was forced into the open, it turned out to be UNGA-corroborated "manifestness" — which B exposed as a headcount that immunizes the strong and exposes the weak, converting A's own gate into B's precedent harm. A never repaired it. A's closing reframe (B spends the money with no threshold) was answered in B's closing via the holding-versus-extinguishing-title distinction and reversibility. B's two clipped turns are a real execution cost, keeping the margin competitive rather than dominant.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 turning A's "manifest aggression corroborated by collective judgment" gate into a liability: a standard that fails 2003 only because the invader could block the vote is a headcount, not a legal test — "great powers are never manifest aggressors; everyone else can be." A had no answer in the closing.</best_rebuttal>
